issues.explanation: 'Flashbacks' is not a Threat item; it is a re-experiencing/memory phenomenon. Within the Threat node it is conceptually misclassified and sits awkwardly with the inactive Memory → Threat edge in the formulation.

For toxic chemical exposure, intense guilt and shame on recall are hard to reconcile unless there is some additional morally injurious element (e.g., causing others' exposure, negligence, or contamination of loved ones), which is not reflected anywhere else in the profile. These emotions are therefore clinically difficult to explain from the given trauma type and the rest of the node content.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, the appraisal that others can visibly see what happened 'just by looking' is hard to reconcile unless there is disfigurement or obvious contamination, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on internal identity change, fear, and avoidance rather than visible marks or social exposure, so this item is clinically hard to explain from the stated trauma alone.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is not impossible after toxic chemical exposure, but in this profile it lacks support from the other selected items. The appraisals focus on identity loss and perceived visible exposure, while the memory items also include grief and terror; without any item about culpability, contamination, humiliation, or causing harm to others, shame is the least coherent affect here and is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
issues.explanation: This appraisal is difficult to reconcile with the trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. It implies a fear-based autonomic danger response more characteristic of assault/combat trauma, whereas the rest of the profile centers on identity disruption, grief/terror on recall, and generalized vigilance. For a chemical exposure case, a more coherent appraisal would focus on contamination, bodily damage, fragility, or permanent harm rather than the body 'reacting as if I am still in danger.' The item is not impossible, but it is the one clinically questionable item in an otherwise coherent profile.
